title: Cover

segs.cue: you've already introduced yourself; start straight on the cover

segs.t: So my project is called Poise. It helps you notice when your posture drifts, without breaking your focus, with a web app and a light bar on your monitor.
I picked this project for two reasons. First, it shows my whole process, from research to testing. Second, I used AI along the way, so I can show how it helped me make decisions.
So, let me walk you through it.

title: We drift without noticing

segs.cue: quick: one short line per press

segs.t: This is how I define the problem in one sentence. We drift without noticing.
At first, we sit up straight.
Then sometimes, we rest our chin on our hand.
Bit by bit, we lean in closer to the screen.
Over time, the neck and lower back start to hurt.
And fixing it later can cost thousands. I've had neck and back pain myself, and spent a lot on physical therapy and a good chair. And I wasn't the only one.

kw: “We drift without noticing.”
Sit up straight
Chin on hand
Lean closer
Neck + lower back hurt
Costs thousands
Me: PT + a good chair
“And I wasn't the only one.”

title: Six hours a day

segs.t: So I looked at some research to see if other people feel the same. The average US adult sits about six hours a day. Up to 63 percent of office workers get neck pain in a year. And back and neck pain is the biggest health cost in the US, about 135 billion dollars.
So yeah, it's not just me.

kw: Research → others too?
6 hours sitting a day
Up to 63% neck pain in a year
$135 billion, biggest health cost
“So yeah, it's not just me.”

title: Survey

segs.t: Then I ran a quick survey with fifteen people.

Three things stood out. Nine out of fifteen rarely notice their posture, or only once it hurts. Fourteen feel pain after a long session, mostly in the neck and lower back. And most of what they'd tried, like stretching or a better chair, comes after. So nothing really catches it early.

kw: Survey, 15 people → three things
9/15 rarely notice, or once it hurts
14 feel pain → neck, lower back
Fixes come after → nothing catches it early

title: Interviews

segs.t: To go deeper, I interviewed three of them.
Paul only notices he's slouching when his lower back starts to hurt.
Hyunjoo bought a Herman Miller chair, but sitting straight for long was still hard.
And Peter leans in when he focuses, and he works in quiet places.
So for Paul, I can help him notice earlier. For Hyunjoo, short breaks to reset. And for Peter, a signal that doesn't interrupt him.

kw: Interviewed three
Paul → notices when lower back hurts
Hyunjoo → Herman Miller, still hard
Peter → leans in, quiet places
Paul → notice earlier
Hyunjoo → short breaks
Peter → signal that doesn't interrupt

title: Market research

segs.t: Next I looked at what's already out there. Posture apps notice early, but they interrupt your work, and chairs and Pilates come after it already hurts. So I wanted to catch it early, without interrupting.

I also like seeing what I can bring in from other services. On DoorDash, I can see my order on the lock screen without opening the app, and Uber, Starbucks and Nike Run Club work the same way. So I could show people their posture live.

Chairs, Pilates → after it hurts
→ catch it early, without interrupting

title: Hypothesis

segs.t: So from all three, I came up with one hypothesis. If people get a clear cue that helps them notice early, with no interruptions, they'll catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer.
For the user, the app tells you when you drift and the light bar changes color, so you notice without stopping your work. And for the business, I keep the app free to try, then offer the light bar.

kw: “From all three, I came up with one hypothesis.”
Clear cue + notice early + no interruptions → catch drift sooner, stay aligned longer
User → app tells you, light changes color
Business → free app, then light bar

title: User flow

segs.t: Here's how it works in five steps.
First, you answer four questions, pick the camera or the sensor, and plug in the light bar.
Then you start working. The app checks your posture and the light stays white.
If you drift, the app shows what changed and the light turns yellow, then red. When you sit back up, it turns green and fades back to white.
When you finish, a report shows how long you sat well.
Then you take a break with stretches or a game, and the light plays along.

kw: Five steps
① 4 questions, camera or sensor, plug in
② Work → light stays white
③ Drift → yellow, red → sit up → green → white
④ Report → how long you sat well
⑤ Break → stretches or game, light plays along

title: Version one, the app

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per part

segs.t: So here's how it works, in four parts.
First, onboarding. I added four questions, like how long you focus and how you like to rest, because I learned from the interviews that everyone works differently.

Next is focus mode. I made a bar that fills as you drift and a light that turns yellow, then red, and green when you sit back up, because I wanted people to notice before it hurts. At the end, a report shows how long they sat well.
Then break mode. I made a figure to follow, and the camera scores how closely you match each stretch, because I thought a short reset helps people sit well again.
And last, settings. I added settings for how long you focus, how sensitive it is, and how soon it alerts you, because I wanted people to set it up the way they like.

kw: “So here's how it works, in four parts.”
Onboarding → 4 questions → fits how each person works
Focus → bar fills, light yellow, red, green → notice before it hurts
End → report, how long they sat well
Break → follow the figure, score, game → break feels fun
Settings → modes, brightness, music in one modal → their way

title: Playtest

segs.t: This is also part of my school project, so I showed my app and the light bar to my classmates, and I mostly watched and took notes.

kw: School project → showed classmates
Mostly watched + took notes

title: What the playtest showed

segs.t: And watching people use it changed what I thought mattered.
On the good side, it caught people slouching before they even noticed, and they loved having options for a break. So it caught drift early, and gave people control.

But from the light alone, they couldn't tell how they moved. Twelve guide steps felt like too much, and some worried what the camera collects. So setup was slow, the light wasn't clear, and the camera felt risky.
And for new ideas, they wanted to just type the mode they want, and keep a small window open while they work. So they wanted it their own way, and always in view.

kw: “Watching people changed what I thought mattered.”
Good → caught slouching before they noticed, break options → early + control
Bad → light alone unclear, 12 steps, camera worry
→ slow setup, unclear light, camera felt risky
New ideas → type the mode, small window
→ their way, always in view

title: Iteration plan

segs.t: So I planned the next version around three changes, from the playtest and my own review.

First, privacy. The app already said the camera never records, but it was too small, so people missed it. So I'll make the modal clearly show how your privacy is protected, and that there's a sensor option too, so people feel safe. The trade off is, the sensor can miss small posture changes.
Next, clearer cues. The light alone wasn't enough, so I'll add a voice and a figure that moves with you, so you know how to fix it. The trade off is, a voice can interrupt you.

And last, people wanted it simpler and more their own. So I'll add a text bar called Ask Poise, and a mini window, so it's quicker to set up and always in view. The trade off is, more features, more to learn.

kw: Three changes, playtest + my review
① Privacy → note too small → modal shows how privacy is protected + sensor option ↔ sensor less accurate
② Clearer cues → light not enough → voice + moving figure ↔ voice can interrupt
③ Simpler, their own → Ask Poise, mini window ↔ more to learn

title: Version two, the app

segs.cue: the recording plays; press once per change

segs.t: So here's version two, with six changes.
First, clearer privacy. I explained up front that the camera never records you, and the sensor only checks how far you sit, because I thought people won't use it if they don't feel safe.
Next, simpler steps. I turned twelve guide steps into four, and moved modes to a small side panel, because I saw that twelve steps was too much before even starting.
Then, easier to notice. I added a figure that moves with you and a voice that tells you how to fix it, because I realized the light alone didn't tell people what to fix.
This is the mini window. I added a small window that stays at the edge of your screen, because people wanted to keep tracking their posture, even while working on other tabs.
And Ask Poise. I added a text field to type what you want instead of opening settings, because people had a hard time finding settings, and wanted to talk to it like AI.
And last, one look and feel. I set clear rules for typography, color and spacing, because I felt the look wasn't consistent after building with AI.

kw: Version two, six changes
① Clearer privacy → explain camera + sensor → feel safe
② Simpler steps → 12 into 4, side panel → start faster
③ Easier to notice → figure + voice → know what to change
④ Mini window → over other tabs → keep tracking
⑤ Ask Poise → just type it → set it up their way
⑥ One look and feel → rules for type, color, spacing → one product

title: Then I measured it

segs.t: Then I tested both versions with the same three people, at their own desks for an hour each.

The one I cared about most was how long they sat well, because my hypothesis was that people would catch the drift sooner and stay aligned longer. It went from 85 to 90 percent. That might sound small, but everyone already sat well most of the time. All three went up, and Peter, who drifted the most, improved the most.
So they sat well longer, and it was easier to use.

kw: Both versions, same 3 people, own desks, 1 hour each
Cared most about how long they sat well
Hypothesis → catch drift sooner, stay aligned longer
Small, but already sat well
All 3 up, Peter most
→ sat well longer, easier to use

title: What I learned using AI

segs.t: Now, what I learned using AI.
In research, I wanted to spend my one month hearing people's stories, so AI found papers and drafted my questions. But judging what fits is still my job.
When building, I wanted a real app within days, so AI coded the app and the Arduino. But only users know if it helps them.
And for testing, AI read the posture data, but I checked the data myself, and caught things the data can't show, like when the voice cut in while Peter was on a call.

So yeah, overall, AI can boost your ideas, but it still needs a human to check and judge its work, because AI can make mistakes, and it can't see the full context or your big picture. So I think the best way to use AI is to treat it as your design assistant that you can discuss ideas with, and not let it do your work for you.
